description: We are engineering students from TED University, Ankara. Last summer one of us worked at TÜBİTAK Space and built an anomaly detector for NASA cFS flight software on a small board with no FPU. Now we want to use the same idea for astronaut health. On Mars, help from Earth can take 20 minutes, so the spacecraft must notice problems by itself. Our system runs on real flight hardware and catches faults that simple limit checks miss.
summary: On the way to Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes one way, and some weeks there is no link at all. If an astronaut's wearable sensor fails, nobody on the ground will notice in time, and a broken sensor can look perfectly normal. A heart-rate sensor that freezes keeps sending a believable number. Every value stays inside its limits, so the standard limit check on the spacecraft says nothing. CrewWatch runs on the spacecraft's own computer. Every second it checks whether each sensor's value is still moving, whether each sensor is still talking, and whether the readings make sense together. When it suspects a sensor, it asks the astronaut to check it by hand: a 15-second pulse count is compared with what the chest strap says, and the astronaut is told which one to trust. The same panel takes the astronaut's own daily check-in (blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood), shows vital signs over time with a color-coded status, radiation exposure, and says in plain words what to do next and when to bring in the crew medical officer. It is written in integer-only C, built on flight software we wrote earlier, so the same input always gives the same alert on any computer. We tested it on real recordings of 15 people and we report where it fails as well as where it works.
details:
What it does

CrewWatch watches five wearable channels: heart rate, heart-rate variability, activity, skin temperature and skin conductance. Every second it builds nine numbers from them:

  • the five levels, each compared with that astronaut's own baseline;
  • HOLD: how many seconds heart rate (and HRV) have not changed at all;
  • AGE: how many seconds since each sensor last sent data.

A Mahalanobis model, stored as a 162-byte table of 8-bit integers, scores these nine numbers together. A second copy of the same model scores their 64-second average. When a score crosses its threshold, CrewWatch shows an alert card, for example:

Heart rate has read exactly 115.9 bpm for 8 s while data keeps arriving (longest seen in normal data: 8 s). Sensor may be frozen: re-seat or restart the chest strap.

Every sentence on the card comes from a number the software measured. CrewWatch never says what is wrong with the astronaut. It says what to check.

How it answers the challenge

The challenge asks for a visual tool that lets astronauts assess their own health and act on it. CrewWatch's panel (web/index.html, works offline) does this for a crew of four:

  • color-coded crew cards (green / amber / red) with heart rate and temperature at a glance;
  • dynamic charts of every indicator over time, with the alert threshold drawn in;
  • an alert card with step-by-step instructions: check the sensor first, then note how you feel and log it for the crew medical officer;
  • a radiation panel (NASA DONKI solar particle events + measured Mars-transit dose rate), and reference panels for bone loss and sleep from published spaceflight studies (not crew data);
  • a "why on board?" box showing the light-time delay to Earth (NASA HRP hazard: distance from Earth);
  • a self check-in for the indicators the challenge names: blood pressure, pulse, oral temperature, blood glucose, hours slept and mood (1–5). Each value is classified against a published threshold (AHA 2017 blood-pressure categories, CDC fever ≥ 38.0 °C, ADA low glucose < 70 / < 54 mg/dL, AASM/SRS ≥ 7 h sleep), shown as a green/amber/red chip, with what to do next. Three low-mood check-ins in a row suggest a private talk with the crew medical officer.

Our main addition is the question that comes before every health judgement: is this reading still true? The check-in closes that loop. When CrewWatch suspects the heart-rate sensor, the alert card asks the astronaut to count their own pulse for 15 seconds. The count is compared with the chest strap at that moment (agree if within 10 bpm or 10 %). In the demo, Crew A counts 25 beats = 100 bpm while the frozen strap still reports 116, and CrewWatch answers: trust your own count, re-seat the strap. The hand count comes from the real recording, not an invented number. The check-in rules are integer-only C, the same code style and the same WebAssembly module as the monitor. A test checks that 5,000 check-ins give identical results on the PC and in the browser.

How we tested it

We did not simulate healthy people. Normal data comes from PPG-DaLiA, real recordings of 15 people going through a normal day (stairs, cycling, walking, driving, eating). We trained on 8 people, tuned thresholds on 3, and kept 4 people aside as our "crew". On top of the crew's real recordings we injected five kinds of problems and compared three monitors. What this tells us:

  • A limit check cannot see a frozen or silent sensor. We saw the same thing on real flight hardware before the hackathon: 316 samples, 0 alarms.
  • A simple "value has not changed" rule catches those faults too, and we say so. CrewWatch does the same job inside one model, reacts faster to a silent sensor, and raised about 8 times fewer false alarms on people it had never seen.
  • When one channel clearly leaves its normal range (bradycardia), the plain limit check wins. The two should run side by side.
  • Slow changes, like a fever building over half an hour, were not caught by any of the three monitors with these wrist sensors at one reading per second. We are not hiding that. It is the next problem to solve.

Why integer-only code matters

The same C code, compiled once for a normal PC and once for a web browser (WebAssembly), produced the same 67,388 scores bit for bit. The panel checks this again every time it opens. The inference engine underneath was measured on a flight-class processor without a floating-point unit in earlier work: bit-exact against the ground computer, and 0.64 % of a one-second time budget. We did not have that board during the hackathon, so CrewWatch itself was not run on it.

The model is updated on the ground. Only the small table is sent to the spacecraft. Nothing is trained in orbit.

What we hope to achieve

NASA's own plans for Mars move medical decisions from Mission Control to the crew (Earth-Independent Medical Operations). Decision-support tools for the crew medical officer depend on sensor data that can be trusted. CrewWatch is a small, checkable layer underneath them. It tells the crew when a sensor stopped telling the truth.

Tools

C (flight inference library tinyinfer, cFS feature code), Python (no machine-learning framework, only the standard library plus numpy for loading the dataset), Emscripten/WebAssembly, plain HTML/JavaScript for the panel (works offline), WSL Ubuntu with gcc.

What existed before the hackathon

The integer inference engine and the cFS feature code were written by a team member during an internship at TÜBİTAK UZAY (July–August 2026) and are open source. We reused them without changes. During the hackathon we built the HOLD feature, the wearable data pipeline, the fault injector, the evaluation, the alert text, the WebAssembly build and the panel. Details: PRIOR_WORK.md.
